name: 手打ちそば屋 かんだた (Kandata)

claims.text: Soba flour blend ratio is not disclosed; most Japanese soba shops use an 80:20 buckwheat-to-wheat blend. Without confirmation of juuwari (100% buckwheat) noodles, wheat cross-contamination in the noodles must be assumed.
The tsuyu is made with soy sauce from Shioya Brewing (塩屋醸造) in Suzaka — a traditional wheat-brewed soy sauce. Wheat is present in all broth-based dishes.
Dashi is made from katsuobushi (bonito), kombu, and soda-gatsuo. Fish-based broth is used throughout; no plant-based broth alternative is documented.

No allergy-handling protocols or allergen menus are mentioned in any source reviewed. An English picture menu exists for ordering, but allergy-specific communication would require Japanese or direct phone inquiry (026-232-3718).
No tempura is served, eliminating the most common fryer cross-contamination risk at soba shops.
Tsuyu is made with no added sugar and all-natural ingredients; vegetables are pesticide-free and grown by the owner.

name: 甘味処 鎌倉 善光寺仲見世通り店 (Kanmidokoro Kamakura Zenkoji Nakamise-dori)

claims.text: No cross-contamination information is published by the brand. The 'proprietary blend' added to hon-warabi-ko is undisclosed, leaving open whether any wheat-containing starch is included. Celiacs should call 026-217-7515 before visiting.
No soy sauce or wheat-based dashi is used in a sweets-only menu; the core warabi mochi allergen declaration lists soy (kinako) only — no wheat allergen declared.
Vanilla ice cream topping and all milk-based warabi mochi drinks contain dairy; ordering plain warabi mochi with kuromitsu and kinako avoids dairy, but shared equipment risk is unknown.
No allergy-handling protocol is described on the official site or any fetched source; direct inquiry by phone or in person is necessary for celiac or severe soy-allergy guests.

Core warabi mochi (hon-warabi-ko + kuromitsu + kinako) lists only soy as an allergen — no wheat allergen declared across the standard eat-in range, making it a notable wheat-free option among traditional Japanese sweets.
Kuromitsu is made from pure Okinawan brown sugar with no additives or corn syrup, and kinako is a single-ingredient roasted soybean powder — minimal ingredient lists reduce hidden-additive risk.
Noodles contain wheat (二八 soba is 20% wheat flour); tempura is battered with wheat flour. Cross-contamination risk is high in a soba kitchen where wheat is used routinely.
Standard tsuyu (dipping broth) is made with katsuo dashi and conventional soy sauce, which contains wheat. No wheat-free soy sauce or tamari alternative is mentioned.
Bonito (katsuo) dashi is central to the broth; reviewers specifically note the strong bonito flavor. No plant-based broth option is offered.
Buckwheat itself is 80% of the noodle composition; those with wheat allergy (not celiac-level intolerance) should confirm with staff, though no allergy protocol is documented.

Noodles are described by reviewers as niwari soba (二八蕎麦) — 80% buckwheat, 20% wheat. No 100% buckwheat (十割) option confirmed. A shared kitchen making wheat-blend noodles and tempura presents high cross-contamination risk for celiac diners.
Tsuyu (soba dipping sauce) at traditional Shinshu soba shops is made with wheat-containing soy sauce (koikuchi shoyu). No tamari or wheat-free soy sauce alternatives mentioned.
Dashi base for tsuyu is almost certainly katsuobushi (dried bonito). No plant-based broth option found. Tempura is offered on the menu, implying shared oil with animal-derived items possible.
No allergy menu, allergy statements, or staff allergy training is mentioned in any source. The food ticket vending machine system means limited opportunity for customization at the counter.
Buckwheat (蕎麦粉) itself is gluten-free; if a 100% buckwheat batch were available, the base grain would be safe — but no such option is confirmed here.

The kitchen produces wheat-containing 二八 soba (20% wheat noodles) alongside the 十割 (100% buckwheat) option. No source documents separate preparation surfaces, water, or equipment for GF noodles. Cross-contamination risk must be assumed until the restaurant confirms otherwise.
The tsuyu is made with traditional Japanese soy sauce (shoyu), which contains wheat. No tamari or gluten-free soy sauce alternative is listed anywhere in available menu or review sources.
The dipping broth is made from soda-gatsuo and kame-bushi (bonito varieties) shaved in-house. No plant-based broth option is documented. All soba dishes appear to be served with fish-stock tsuyu.

No information on allergy-handling protocols is available from any reviewed source. The restaurant does accept reservations by phone (026-232-2492), which would be the appropriate channel to ask about dietary needs in advance.

A daily limited run of 十割そば (100% buckwheat noodles, wheat-free ingredient) is available, making it a starting point for discussion with the kitchen for gluten-sensitive diners who can tolerate shared-kitchen risk.

name: 古民家dining BAR GOFUKU (Kominka Dining BAR GOFUKU)

claims.text: No dedicated gluten-free preparation area or protocol is mentioned anywhere. This is a full dining-bar kitchen handling pasta, quiche, beer-battered or marinated meats, and wheat soy sauce as standard ingredients.
Standard soy sauce (wheat-containing) is assumed to be used throughout the kitchen; no tamari or GF soy sauce alternative is mentioned on any menu or review source.
Rotisserie chicken, jerk chicken, and garlic shrimp are core menu items; butter and dairy appear in lunch sets. No separation of vegan prep is indicated.
Search results indicate the restaurant can accommodate food allergies when notified in advance, but no formal allergy menu or written protocol has been confirmed.
English menu available, lowering the communication barrier for allergy discussions with staff.

name: 根元 八幡屋礒五郎 本店 (Kongen Yawataya Isogoro Honten)

claims.text: No dedicated gluten-free kitchen or fryer confirmed. The café serves wheat-containing curries and baked goods (macarons, cheesecake, pancakes) alongside the gelato, raising cross-contamination risk for celiac diners.
Curries and savory dishes at Yokocho Cafe likely use standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat. No tamari or GF soy sauce alternative is mentioned on any menu or source.

The gelato is the only confirmed egg-free item; it is prepared in a kitchen that also handles dairy-based cheesecakes, butter chicken curry, and egg-containing baked goods. No vegan-only prep area is documented.

Staff at the Yokocho Cafe confirmed to one visitor that the green curry can be modified to remove prawns for vegetarian guests, suggesting some willingness to accommodate requests — but no formal allergy protocol or English allergen menu has been documented.
The spice gelato is confirmed to contain no eggs (unlike all other desserts on the menu), making it the clearest plant-based option for vegan visitors.
The shichimi spice blends sold in the retail shop are plant-based ingredients (chili, sesame, hemp, citrus peel, etc.) with no animal products.

The kitchen routinely handles wheat flour in soba (ni-hachi blend), udon, and tempura batter. Shared cooking surfaces and utensils make cross-contamination unavoidable. This is not a safe environment for celiac diners.
The dipping tsuyu is a concentrated soy-sauce-based broth (shoyu is wheat-containing); no tamari or gluten-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned.

Fish-based dashi (katsuobushi, saba-bushi, urume-bushi) is the foundation of all broths and dipping sauces. Duck is a signature ingredient. No plant-based broth or vegan-specific preparation is available.
Staff ask about allergies before preparing udon orders and cook udon in a separate, dedicated pot when an allergy is declared — indicating awareness of cross-contamination risk.
The house dashi is made without chemical additives or preservatives, using only natural dried fish and Rishiri kombu.
